catalog_entry.label: NFL score-path functionals (largest lead, lead changes, comebacks)
catalog_entry.target: Whether the path of the score in one game (largest lead, count of lead changes, a comeback of N or more points) reaches a threshold.
catalog_entry.mechanism: The outcome is a functional of the whole sequence of scores, not of final totals. A possession-by-possession process (drive outcomes, point values, non-offensive scores, end-of-half clock behaviour) generates the margin path; the largest lead is its running absolute maximum, a lead change is a sign change of the margin caused by a score by the team that was tied or trailing (the opening score excluded), and a 24-point comeback is the eventual winner's running minimum reaching -24. Each depends on expected margin, path volatility and score-state-dependent coaching, so a final-margin distribution alone cannot price them.

inputs.why: The only input that turns team rates into a drive-by-drive score sequence, which is what a running-maximum lead, a count of sign changes and a 24-point deficit all need.
Supplies the market-free pregame team strength gap that sets the expected margin around which the path wanders, and the comeback-probability asymmetry between favourite and underdog.
Gives the conditional spread of the final margin given model mean and total, which scales the volatility of the path and the heaviness of the lead tail.
Per-drive touchdown/field-goal/punt/turnover probabilities by drive index and start field position feed the possession generator and the early-game lead formation.
Point values of a score (6+1, 6+2, 6+0, 3, 2) decide whether a lead of 7 versus 8 occurs, so band edges such as '7 to 10' depend on the extra-point and two-point policy.
Defensive and special-teams scores add 6- to 8-point jumps with no possession alternation; they create abrupt lead changes and deep deficits.
Second-half scoring conditional on the halftime margin tells how a deficit decays or grows, the mechanism that either allows or kills a 24-point comeback.
Two-minute drill scoring and timeouts create the late lead changes and tying drives at the end of each half.
Go-for-it and kick decisions when trailing late change both the chance of the deficit shrinking and which score types occur.
Fits the blowout tail above 21 points, the region where largest-lead bands beyond 17 and the 24-point deficit set up.
Kneel-downs, kick-to-tie and go-for-two policies late in tight games decide whether a lead change occurs or the game stays level.
Probability mass of a 14+ point fourth-quarter lead, the state in which the leading team runs the clock and the lead stops changing.
Starter status changes team strength by several points and widens the margin spread; a backup quarterback shifts both the expected lead and the variance.
Pass-rate and pace conditional on lead or trail feed back into drive counts, shortening a game when a leader runs and lengthening it when a trailing team hurries.
Wind and cold lower scoring and passing, reducing the number of scores and hence lead changes and the speed of separation.
Sampled rules text fixes the counted object, thresholds, first-score and penalty clauses and what is left unstated (overtime, postponement, source), so settlement is read from it and not assumed.
In-game injury exit risk of the starting quarterback changes comeback and lead-change odds from the exit onward, a path event that pregame ratings cannot see.
Quarterback-specific hazard of leaving before the end of the game, by lead size, clock and mobility, used to switch the trailing or leading team to a backup in the simulated path.
Overtime points increment and probability by rule era: the only attached input that models whether and how overtime changes scores, needed for the regulation-only versus full-game readings.
Probability that a game ends level after overtime, which decides whether a game that was tied late can still produce a comeback win or a lead change.
Drive-result probabilities by start position over all drives, supplying mid- and late-game drive rates that the first-four-drives input does not cover.
Opponent-adjusted per-drive TD and FG rates by period, so the generator uses period-specific scoring for the 10-12 drives of a game and not only early-game rates.
Expected drives per team set the number of possessions in the simulated path and feed the market-free score-state input; without it the possession count is undefined.

interactions.hypothesis: A lopsided expected margin produces a large largest lead and few lead changes while a coin-flip game with a high total produces many lead changes and a small largest lead; the two contracts are negatively dependent through the margin and the volatility together, so pricing them from separate marginals misstates joint exposure.
interactions.how_to_test: Cross-tabulate realised lead changes against largest-lead bands within expected-margin bins in 2012-2025 games and compare with the simulator's joint output.

interactions.hypothesis: A deficit of 17+ at the half is recovered only if the trailing coach goes for fourth downs and two-point tries and the leader's scoring slows; second-half scoring by the trailing side rises with deficit while the aggressive-coach effect matters most between 14 and 24 points, so the comeback curve depends on the coach's policy beyond team strength.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress second-half points of the trailing team on halftime deficit bins interacted with the coach's fourth-down go rate, using 2012-2025 games with a deficit of at least 14 at the half.

interactions.hypothesis: One defensive touchdown moves the margin by 6 to 8 points at once; in a game already past a two-score lead it can restore a game that blowout script had settled, so lead-change and comeback odds rise discontinuously when a non-offensive score arrives against a leading team that is running out the clock.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare lead-change counts and comeback frequency in games with and without a defensive or special-teams score while the lead was 14 or more.

interactions.hypothesis: At the end of a half the game switches from clock-managed play to a hurry-up regime in which a trailing team can score twice quickly and a tied team can kneel; lead changes concentrate in these windows, and the regime is entered only when the score is within one possession.
interactions.how_to_test: Count lead changes by game-clock window and margin state in 2012-2025 play-by-play and test whether the last two minutes of each half hold a disproportionate share.

interactions.hypothesis: A backup quarterback lowers the rating of one team and raises the volatility of the path; the comeback probability then depends on whether the weaker side is the one that trails, so the same rating gap gives a different comeback tail when the weak team is the underdog with a backup than when the favourite has one.
interactions.how_to_test: Stratify comeback and largest-lead outcomes by backup-quarterback flag and favourite/underdog role in 2012-2025 games.

contract.settlement_definition: Three series, all sampled for the Seattle vs New England game 'originally scheduled for Feb 8, 2026'. KXNFLLARGELEAD settles Yes when the largest lead held by either team at any time falls in the stated band ('between 7 to 10 points', floor_strike 7, strike_type between). KXNFLLEADCHANGE settles Yes when the combined count of lead changes is at least 8; per the secondary text a lead change is a team, trailing or tied, scoring to take the lead, and the first score does not count. KXNFLCOMEBACK settles Yes only if either team trails by at least 24 at any point and then wins the game; a tie or loss does not count (stated in the sampled secondary text as winning the game). No sampled text for these series mentions overtime, ties after overtime, postponement, or, in the sampled rules text, a data source (series metadata reportedly names one); the rules_secondary of LARGELEAD and the 'originally scheduled' wording give no postponement rule, so those items are unresolved, not inferred.

rules_evidence.quote: A lead change in football occurs when one team, trailing or tied, scores to take a lead over the opposing team. The first score of the game does not count as a lead change.
rules_evidence.establishes: Lead changes count only scores that move a team from tied or trailing into the lead, excluding the opening score, so a count of 8 needs at least nine lead-taking scores in the whole sequence and 0-0 to first lead never counts.

rules_evidence.quote: Seattle or New England must trail by at least the specified point threshold at any point in the game and go on to win the game for this market to resolve to Yes.
rules_evidence.establishes: The comeback is a running-minimum event for the eventual winner: a 24-point deficit at any time followed by a win; a tie or loss never resolves Yes however large the recovery.

rules_evidence.quote: If the teams in the game have a largest lead of between 7 to 10 points
rules_evidence.establishes: Settles on the single largest lead either team held at any time, as a band; the strike_type is 'between' with floor_strike 7, so inclusivity of the 10 end and treatment of an overtime lead are not stated.

variants_and_edge_cases: KXNFLLARGELEAD is a band ('between 7 to 10 points'); whether both ends are inclusive and whether a lead established only in overtime counts are not stated; the band sits on lattice atoms (7, 8, 9, 10), so inclusivity changes the price materially.

KXNFLLEADCHANGE counts a lead change when a team 'trailing or tied' scores to take a lead, and the first score of the game does not count. Read literally, a team that led, was tied and then retakes the lead has made a lead change; the example 7-0, 7-7, 14-7 yields one lead change (the 14-7 score). Whether Kalshi counts a retaken lead is not stated and not verified (u4).
KXNFLCOMEBACK requires trailing by the threshold 'at any point in the game' and winning; a game that ends tied cannot resolve Yes, and the deficit is a point-margin deficit of the eventual winner.

None of the three sampled texts states an overtime, postponement or abandonment rule or a source of truth; every sample is a finalized historical market for the Feb 8, 2026 game, and live regular-season listings may differ (CONTRACT_AMBIGUOUS, u1).
contract.settlement_data_source: Not named in the three sampled rules texts; the official league scoring summary and play-by-play are implied for the score sequence. Kalshi series metadata is reported by reviewers (not in contract_rules_sample.json, not verified by me) to name settlement sources (the league, ESPN; Fox Sports for KXNFLNONQBPASS).

mechanism.summary: These contracts settle on functionals of the score path, so the object to model is the time-ordered list of scores, not the final score. The chain starts with a pregame margin and volatility (team strength gap, expected total, quarterback and weather shocks), generates possession-by-possession scores with point packages and a rare non-offensive scoring process, reads the largest lead, lead-change count and 24-point deficit off the path, adds the feedback that makes trailing teams gamble and leading teams run the clock, and finishes with end-of-regulation behaviour and the unstated overtime treatment. The three series respond to the same inputs with different signs: a larger expected margin raises the largest lead and lowers the lead-change count, while a high total and a small spread raise lead changes; a 24-point comeback needs a strong side that falls far behind and then recovers, a rare tail of the volatility and coach-policy mixture.

stages.name: Pregame margin and volatility: the box the path lives in
stages.description: Before any score, the model needs the expected margin from market-free team ratings, the expected total (how many scoring chances there are), and the conditional spread of the final margin. A quarterback change, wind or a dome shifts both the mean gap and the volatility. The expected margin sets the typical size of the largest lead; the spread sets how heavy the lead tail is and how often a weak side can be 24 down yet win. These three quantities are the same for all three series but enter them with opposite signs: a bigger gap lengthens the largest lead and shortens the lead-change count.
stages.distribution: Margin approximately mixture-normal with sd 12-14 and heavier tails when a backup quarterback or severe weather is present; total points 40-50 with right skew

stages.name: Possession-by-possession score generator
stages.description: Each team's possessions are generated in alternation starting from the opening kick; each drive ends in touchdown, field goal, punt, turnover, safety or end of half with probabilities by drive index and start field position, and each score carries its point package (extra point, two-point try, no try after a missed kick). Defensive and special-teams scores are added as a separate rare jump process that does not need possession alternation. The output is a time-ordered list of scores, which is the object the three contracts are defined on, so a final score alone cannot reproduce lead changes or largest lead. Opening drives use nfl.drive_outcome_by_index (first four drives only); later drives use the all-drive lattice and period rates. nfl.script is context only (its measurement was re-based on own-model margins in round 3).
stages.distribution: Drives per team 10-12; each drive scores with probability around 0.35-0.45; point increments lattice {2,3,6,7,8} with atoms; scoring events are positively dependent through pace and weather

stages.name: Running functionals of the margin path
stages.description: From the simulated score list the three settlement quantities are read off directly. The largest lead is the maximum over time of the absolute margin; a lead change is counted whenever a scoring team moves from tied or trailing to ahead, except the first score of the game; a comeback win is the winning team's minimum margin being at most -24. Because these are path statistics, two simulated games with the same final score can resolve differently. The simulator must therefore be calibrated against the empirical joint distribution of largest lead, lead changes and final margin, not only against final margins.
stages.distribution: Largest lead right-skewed with lumps at 3, 7, 8, 10, 14; lead changes overdispersed count mostly 0-4 with a thin tail; a 24-point comeback win is a rare Bernoulli whose probability is an unverified placeholder to recount from 2000-2025 play-by-play

stages.name: Score-state feedback: leaders run, trailers gamble
stages.description: Behaviour changes with the score. A team with a large lead runs the ball and shortens the game, which caps further lead changes and freezes the largest lead; a trailing team passes more, goes for fourth downs and two-point tries and hurries, which raises its scoring rate but also its turnover rate. The quarterback may be pulled in a blowout, which changes a comeback's feasibility late. These responses make the path non-Markov in the margin alone and are coach and quarterback specific, so second-half scoring must be conditioned on halftime margin and on the coach's go-for-it policy. A quarterback who leaves the game (injury or blowout pull) switches the team to a backup mid-path, modelled with nfl.qb_blowout_pull_hazard and nfl.in_game_exit_risk. nfl.garbage_time (spread/total-derived) appears only as benchmark context and nfl.script as own-model-margin context. The market-free state distribution and response curves come from nfl.market_free_score_state_blowout_mass; nfl.script and nfl.garbage_time are kept as benchmark or context only.
stages.distribution: Second-half scoring of the trailing side rises with deficit then plateaus; leader scoring falls with lead; mixture of two regimes (within one possession and out of reach)

stages.name: End of regulation, ties and overtime
stages.description: Late in close games the possessing team may kneel, kick to tie or try for the lead, and the rules for ties and overtime decide whether the path continues. Lead-change and comeback counts could be changed by an overtime score, but the sampled rules for these three series say nothing about overtime, so the model must carry both readings (regulation only versus full game) and report both until Kalshi text settles it. A game ending level cannot resolve a comeback Yes. Lead changes in overtime count as lead changes only if the settlement counts the whole game.
stages.distribution: Probability of ending regulation level is an unverified placeholder to recompute from results; overtime adds 0-3 scores; the reading choice moves lead-change probabilities in close games by an amount not yet measured

nfl.score_path_sequence_sim.label: Drive-sequence score-path simulation: largest lead, lead changes and comeback events
nfl.score_path_sequence_sim.mechanism: Simulates the alternating drive sequence of both teams with per-drive outcomes and point values, recording the full in-game margin path so path functionals (maximum lead, lead changes, minimum margin of the eventual winner) can be read.
nfl.score_path_sequence_sim.rationale: Final-score models cannot price path contracts: two games with the same final margin can have zero or eight lead changes. The path depends on drive-outcome probabilities by team, on the alternation of possessions, on state-dependent play calling (trailing teams pass and go for it, leaders run clock) and on point values (7, 3, 8, 6, 2), so a simulation that conditions each drive on the current score state is required.
nfl.score_path_sequence_sim.measurement: For each game: possessions alternate starting from the coin-toss winner; drive outcome multinomial (TD, FG, turnover, punt, safety, end of half) from team offence vs opposing defence rates (nfl.drive_outcome_by_index style, opponent-adjusted, last 16 games with half-life 8, shrink k=150 drives) modified by score state (lead or trail by 0-8, 9-16, 17+) and time remaining using 2012-2025 state multipliers; points per TD from nfl.scoring_event_point_values; 20,000 simulated games; outputs per game: distribution of max |margin|, number of lead changes (excluding first score), P(eventual winner trailed by >=24), calibrated against 2012-2025 realised frequencies by own-rating expected-margin and expected-total bucket (nfl.own_rating_game_state_prior; no sportsbook spread or total). As-of kickoff.

nfl.market_free_score_state_blowout_mass.label: Market-free score-state and blowout-mass distribution from team ratings and drive-level rates
nfl.market_free_score_state_blowout_mass.mechanism: Distribution of the in-game score state (lead or deficit size by quarter and time spent in each state) and the blowout mass (probability of a 14+ point fourth-quarter lead, of a 21+ point margin at any time) produced by simulating drives from own team ratings, together with state-conditional pass rate, pace and starter-exit response curves estimated from play-by-play.
nfl.market_free_score_state_blowout_mass.rationale: Largest lead, lead changes and comebacks depend on how often and how long a game sits in a lopsided or close state and how teams behave there. The existing script and garbage-time inputs are measured from betting spread and total, so they cannot serve a market-free path model; this input rebuilds the same quantities from team strength and drive-level rates so the state distribution does not inherit the market's view.
nfl.market_free_score_state_blowout_mass.measurement: Step 1, state distribution: per game, take opponent-adjusted offence and defence points per drive for both sides from nfl.own_team_rating_market_free (ratings with preseason prior, as of kickoff), drives per team from nfl.drives, and simulate 20,000 score paths with the drive-result probabilities of nfl.drive_result_lattice and the point package of nfl.scoring_event_point_values; record margin and remaining time at each drive boundary. Output P(|margin| >= 14 at the start of the fourth quarter), P(|margin| >= 21 at any time), expected fraction of second-half snaps by margin bin {<=-17, -16..-9, -8..-1, 0, 1..8, 9..16, >=17}. Step 2, response curves: from nflverse play-by-play 2015-2025 estimate pass rate over expected, seconds per play, rush attempts per drive and starting-quarterback exit hazard by the same margin bins and quarter, shrunk to the league cell with k=200 plays per cell and a team and coach offset (half-life 3 seasons); use the actual game state at each play, never a spread or total. Step 3, feedback: feed Step 2 curves back into the simulation of Step 1 for the second half and iterate once. Calibration target: empirical frequency of 14+ point fourth-quarter leads and 21+ point margins in 2012-2025 games by bins of the own-model expected margin, not closing lines. The schedule table's spread and total columns must be dropped before use. As-of kickoff, mixing over the starting-quarterback scenarios of nfl.qb.

nfl.market_free_score_state_blowout_mass.why: Gives the path model a market-free score-state and blowout-mass distribution so that nfl.script and nfl.garbage_time (both spread/total-derived) can be benchmarks only.

nfl.own_team_rating_market_free.reason: Expected margin is the first-order driver of largest lead and of who can come back; a market-free rating is required so the model is not anchored on prices.

nfl.heteroskedastic_margin_sd.reason: Path volatility is not constant: backup quarterback, wind and dome change the margin spread, which moves largest-lead bands more than the mean does.

nfl.drive_outcome_by_index.reason: Scope is the first four drives of a game (drive index and start position), so it covers the opening of the path only; mid- and late-game drive rates come from nfl.drive_result_lattice and nfl.period_drive_scoring_rates.

nfl.scoring_event_point_values.reason: The largest-lead band contract is sensitive to lattice masses at 7, 8, 9 and 10, which are products of scoring packages.

nfl.non_offensive_scoring_rate.reason: Pick-sixes and kick returns break the drive-by-drive alternation, so the sequence simulator needs a separate rare jump process.

nfl.halftime_state_conditional_scoring.reason: Comeback and late lead-change counts hinge on score-state-conditional scoring; the conditional curve is estimated from halftime margin bins.

nfl.two_minute_tempo.reason: The catalog measurement combined end-of-half behaviour with expected lead and trail states from the betting spread; round 4 patched it to use the own-model margin distribution, so it is market-free once the patch is applied. Role stays secondary.

nfl.fourth_down_fg_decision_rate.reason: Trailing-team decisions turn a deficit into a comeback only when the coach goes for touchdowns and two-point tries; this policy is coach specific.

nfl.deep_tail_margin_model.reason: The generalized-Pareto tail of margins is the reference against which the path simulator's deep deficits are calibrated.

nfl.late_tie_game_management.reason: A lead change needs a scoring team to move from tied or trailing to ahead; late-game management decides whether such a score is attempted.

nfl.garbage_time.reason: MARKET-DERIVED: the catalog measurement builds this from betting spread and total, so it is not a market-free input; kept only as a benchmark or context for blowout mass and not as a driver of the market-free path; the market-free blowout tail is nfl.deep_tail_margin_model. A market-free re-measurement from nfl.own_team_rating_market_free is not defined (u5).

nfl.qb.reason: Quarterback availability is the largest single pregame shock to the expected margin and to path volatility.

nfl.script.reason: The catalog measurement of nfl.script was centred on the betting spread and total; it was patched in round 3 to integrate over the own-model margin distribution (nfl.model_team_points_mean, nfl.heteroskedastic_margin_sd), so it is market-free once the patch is applied. Kept as context for possession counts and call mix, not as a driver.

nfl.weather_pit.reason: Weather works through score volume; it matters mostly for lead-change counts, which need many scores.

m.rules_text.reason: Settlement wording is the only authority on what counts; attached to the catalog entry so that stage and coverage claims rest on an input the archetype holds.

nfl.in_game_exit_risk.reason: Position-agnostic exit probability; used for the quarterback exit scenario together with the QB-specific pull hazard.

nfl.qb_blowout_pull_hazard.reason: Covers blowout pulls and quarterback injury exits, which garbage-time mass alone does not.

nfl.ot_total_increment.reason: Overtime scoring is modelled by rule era; whether Kalshi counts overtime scores is unstated, so both readings are carried.

nfl.ot_ending_hazard.reason: Separates games that end in a win from level overtime endings; relevant to the win requirement of the comeback contract.

nfl.drive_result_lattice.reason: Fills the scope gap of nfl.drive_outcome_by_index (first four drives); mid- and late-game drives need a lattice over all drive indices.

nfl.period_drive_scoring_rates.reason: Provides opponent adjustment beyond the early drives.

nfl.drives.reason: Possessions per game bound the number of scores and so the lead-change and largest-lead tails; attached because the score-state input reads it.

nonlinearities.shape: approximately geometric decay in the required deficit for a comeback win
nonlinearities.why: The chance that the eventual winner has trailed by at least d points falls roughly by a constant factor with each additional scoring unit of deficit, so the 24-point comeback tail is extremely sensitive to the strength gap and to scoring volatility and cannot be linearly extrapolated from 14- or 17-point comebacks.

nonlinearities.shape: lumpy lattice masses at multiples of 3, 6, 7 and 8
nonlinearities.why: The largest-lead distribution has atoms at football scoring combinations, so a band such as 7 to 10 captures several of these atoms and shifts sharply with small changes in extra-point or two-point rates rather than varying smoothly with the mean margin.

nonlinearities.shape: saturating: trailing teams' second-half scoring rises with deficit and then plateaus once the game is out of reach
nonlinearities.why: Beyond roughly three possessions of deficit the trailing team's scoring stops rising because clock and opponent strategy limit it, which bounds the comeback probability above the value a linear script response would give.

catalog_entry.label: NFL rare play-call events (non-QB pass, goal-line pass)
catalog_entry.target: Whether a named rare play call (a pass attempt by a non-quarterback, a pass attempt from on or inside the 1-yard line) occurs at least once in one game.
catalog_entry.mechanism: Each contract is the occurrence of a discretionary, low-frequency play call at least once in a game, a hazard of opportunities times a coach- and situation-specific call probability. For the 1-yard pass the opportunities are snaps with the line of scrimmage on or inside the opponent's 1 (drives reaching the goal line and fourth-and-goal decisions) and the call is a pass rather than a sneak or power run; for the non-quarterback pass the opportunities are the offence's snaps and the call is a trick play (receiver or back throws, fake kicks thrown by a non-quarterback) or an emergency throw after the quarterback leaves. Coach random effects, quarterback mobility and availability, and stakes dominate; team production counts do not.

inputs.why: Team- and coach-level base rates of non-quarterback pass attempts and of pass attempts from the 1-yard line, the two events the series settle on.
Dropback rate by zone and down for goal-to-go snaps, the base probability that a snap from the 1 is a pass.
Goal-line package and sneak/carry/target shares inside the 5 show how a team uses heavy sets, a mobile quarterback or tight-end targets at the 1.
Go-for-it policy on 4th-and-goal decides how many snaps from the 1 occur and in which down-and-distance, since a team that kicks removes snaps.
Head coach and coordinator tendencies (neutral pass rate, aggression, two-point rate) are the random effect that explains who calls trick plays and goal-line passes.
Starting quarterback's mobility and goal-line sneak habit, and the chance a backup or wide receiver throws if the starter leaves, enter both series.
In-game exit risk of the quarterback creates the scenario where a non-quarterback attempts a pass or a backup QB listed at another position throws.
Red-zone entries and goal-to-go drive counts determine how many snaps from the opponent's 1-yard line a team gets.
Starting field position and return units change how often drives start deep in opposing territory and so how often the 1-yard line is reached.
Red-zone and goal-line usage shares show which players receive the ball at the 1, informing both quarterback sneak share and target share on goal-line passes.
Formation and personnel mix (motion, play-action, trick formations) help identify direct snaps, wildcat looks and jump-ball sets that precede non-quarterback passes.
Opposing goal-line defensive personnel and tendencies affect whether the offence runs, throws or tries a trick.
Score state and clock affect pass calls at the 1: trailing teams late call more passes and fake plays, leading teams run.
Playoff seeding and elimination stakes are the closest available proxy for must-win aggression, though no tested link to trick-play rates exists.
Sampled rules text fixes the counted object, thresholds, first-score and penalty clauses and what is left unstated (overtime, postponement, source), so settlement is read from it and not assumed.
End-of-half hurry-up and clock management, the situation in which a quarterback spike on or inside the 1 can occur, which is a clock decision and not a pass call.
Quarterback-specific hazard of leaving the game by lead size, clock and mobility; the exit event that can put a non-quarterback in as the emergency passer.
Probabilities that a team's QB1 and QB2 slots are filled by named players, which tells who the emergency passer would be and whether a backup is listed at another position.
Defines end-of-half goal-line snap exposure and spike probability for the spike stage, which nfl.two_minute_tempo does not measure.

interactions.hypothesis: The probability that a snap from the 1 is a pass depends on coach and personnel together: a coordinator who likes play-action from heavy sets throws far more than the team's overall pass rate suggests, while a mobile quarterback with a sneak habit suppresses it, so the coach effect only shows up conditional on the personnel group on the field.
interactions.how_to_test: Fit a logistic model of pass on snaps from the 1 with coach random effects interacted with personnel group and quarterback mobility, 2015-2025.

interactions.hypothesis: Expected pass attempts from the 1 per game equal the number of snaps reaching the 1 times the pass share; the snap count is a product of drives reaching goal-to-go and the willingness to run another snap or go for it on fourth down, so strong red-zone offences with conservative fourth-down coaches generate fewer such snaps than raw red-zone trips suggest.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress team-game counts of snaps from the 1 on red-zone trips and fourth-and-goal go rate, then test the product term against additive terms.

interactions.hypothesis: Non-quarterback pass attempts come from two regimes: planned trick plays, which depend on the coach, and emergency throws after the quarterback leaves, which depend on injury and depth; a game with a hurt or banged-up starter switches from the planned regime to a higher-hazard emergency regime that coach-based base rates do not capture.
interactions.how_to_test: Split 2015-2025 non-QB pass attempts into planned (quarterback present) and emergency (quarterback absent in game) and compare per-game rates by regime.

interactions.hypothesis: Aggressive and unusual calls rise when a coach faces a must-win or when trailing late; below a threshold of stakes and deficit the call mix follows the neutral tendency, above it a trick play or goal-line pass becomes worth its variance, so the effect is a threshold in stakes and score state rather than a smooth tilt.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare non-QB pass and goal-line pass rates for the same coaches in playoff and eliminated/must-win regular-season games versus others, controlling for score differential.

contract.settlement_definition: Two series, both sampled for the Seattle vs New England game 'originally scheduled for Feb 8, 2026'. KXNFLNONQBPASS settles Yes if a non-QB (by either team) records at least 1 pass attempt in the game (floor_strike 0.5, strike_type greater). KXNFL1YDPASS settles Yes if the named team records at least 1 official forward pass attempt with the line of scrimmage on or inside the opponent's 1-yard line at the snap; sacks, scrambles and runs do not count, the dropback depth or release point does not matter, and an attempt nullified by penalty still counts if it is officially recorded in the play-by-play. No sampled text states overtime handling, postponement, who counts as a 'non-QB', or a named data source in the rules text beyond the official play-by-play for the 1-yard series (series metadata reportedly names one).

rules_evidence.quote: The yard line for this market is based on the line of scrimmage at the snap; the quarterback’s dropback depth or release point does not affect settlement.
rules_evidence.establishes: Eligibility is the line of scrimmage at the snap (on or inside the 1), not where the throw occurs, so only snaps from the 1 count and a deep dropback does not matter.

rules_evidence.quote: A pass attempt still counts even if the play is nullified by penalty, provided the pass attempt is officially recorded in the play-by-play.
rules_evidence.establishes: Penalty-nullified pass attempts count when the play-by-play records them, so the settlement is the official statistic rather than the final distribution of plays.

rules_evidence.quote: If a non-QB records at least 1 pass attempt in the Seattle vs New England professional football game
rules_evidence.establishes: A single pass attempt by any non-quarterback by both teams combined settles Yes; the text does not define 'non-QB' (roster position at the time versus player role on the play) or say whether overtime or a punter's or holder's thrown pass counts.

variants_and_edge_cases: KXNFL1YDPASS is a team-specific event for one named team (Seattle in the sample), whereas KXNFLNONQBPASS is a both-team event; the same rare-call model applies per team and the both-team event is the union over two teams.

The 1-yard eligibility uses the line of scrimmage at the snap, so a pass from the 2 thrown to the end zone does not count, and a pass from the 1 nullified by penalty counts if recorded in the play-by-play.

KXNFL1YDPASS excludes sacks, scrambles and run plays but is silent on a quarterback spike on or inside the 1; whether a spike (commonly logged as an incomplete pass) counts is not stated and not verified (u4).

KXNFLNONQBPASS does not define 'non-QB': a backup quarterback listed at another position, a punter or holder's fake-kick throw and a wide receiver option pass are candidate cases; the settlement presumably follows the passer position but this is not stated.

Both samples are finalized historical markets for the Feb 8, 2026 Seattle vs New England game with empty secondary text for NONQBPASS; overtime, postponement and source clauses are unstated and no regular-season live listing was sampled.
contract.settlement_data_source: KXNFL1YDPASS refers to the play-by-play ('officially recorded in the play-by-play'); KXNFLNONQBPASS names no source in its sampled rules text. Kalshi series metadata is reported by reviewers (not in contract_rules_sample.json, not verified by me) to name settlement sources (the league, ESPN; Fox Sports for KXNFLNONQBPASS).

mechanism.summary: Both contracts ask whether a discretionary, low-frequency play call happens at least once in a game. For the 1-yard pass the chain is: how many snaps the offence takes from on or inside the opponent's 1 (drive success, short fields, fourth-and-goal policy), then the probability that a snap from the 1 is a pass (coach and personnel, quarterback mobility, down and clock), then the settlement rule (official forward pass attempt, nullified plays counted). For the non-quarterback pass it is the union of a planned trick-play hazard (coach trait, big-game aggression) and an emergency hazard after a quarterback exit, mapped to the official passer position. The outcome is Bernoulli with a small mean, so P(Yes) is nearly linear in the per-game rate; the main uncertainty is the heavy-tailed coach distribution and thin samples, not mean offensive efficiency.

stages.name: Supply of snaps from the 1-yard line
stages.description: A 1-yard pass attempt requires the offence to snap the ball on or inside the opponent's 1. That happens when a drive reaches goal-to-go from a long gain, a turnover or return gives a short field, or a penalty or failed first and second-down runs leave the offence at the 1. The count of such snaps per team-game is small (typically zero to three) and depends on red-zone trip volume, field position, and the offence's reluctance to settle for a field goal on fourth-and-goal. The opportunity count therefore varies with drive success and with the coach's fourth-and-goal policy.
stages.distribution: Snaps from the 1 per team-game: zero-inflated small count, mean around 0.6-0.9 per team (to recount), overdispersed by team style

stages.name: Pass versus run call at the goal line
stages.description: Given a snap from the 1, the offence chooses among a quarterback sneak, a power run, a play-action throw to a tight end or a quick fade. The choice reflects coach play-calling style, personnel on the field (heavy sets raise runs), quarterback mobility and sneak habit, opposing goal-line personnel, down (a third-down throw is more common than a first-down throw) and clock. The pass share at exactly the 1 is much lower than the team's goal-to-go pass rate from the 5, so rates must be measured at the 1. Settlement counts any official pass attempt, including one nullified by penalty.
stages.distribution: Per-snap pass probability roughly 0.15-0.35 at the 1 (to estimate), strongly coach dependent; Bernoulli per snap, summed to a zero-heavy count per game

stages.name: Non-quarterback pass attempts: planned trick plays and emergency throws
stages.description: A non-quarterback attempt arises from a planned play (a halfback or wide receiver option pass, a fake punt or field goal thrown by the punter or holder, a direct snap) whose frequency is a coach trait, or from an emergency (the quarterback is injured and a receiver is the emergency passer, a backup quarterback listed at another position throws). The planned regime is a low-rate hazard with coach random effects and rises in big games or close finishes; the emergency regime is driven by in-game exit risk of the quarterback and by the depth chart. The event definition depends on roster position labels, which can differ from Kalshi's wording. The emergency regime uses the quarterback-specific pull hazard and the QB depth slot model; no input identifies which receiver or back would be the emergency passer (u5).
stages.distribution: Per team-game rate of at least one non-QB attempt: the catalog measurement uses about 0.15 per team-game as an unverified placeholder to recompute from 2015-2025 play-by-play (so both teams combined is roughly 0.28 if independent); concentration in a minority of coaches is an assumption, not a measured fact

stages.name: Script, stakes and opposing team
stages.description: Both events are modulated by game state: a trailing team at the end of a half or game takes more variance (fake plays, quick throws at the 1), a team with a lead runs, and stakes (playoff, must-win) are widely assumed to raise unusual calls but have not been measured. The opposing team's goal-line stand rate and personnel change the number of snaps from the 1 and the call. These are second-order modulations on top of coach-specific rates and must be estimated with coach random effects, not league-wide slopes, because samples are tiny.
stages.distribution: Multiplicative modulation of the per-game hazard by factors of about 0.7 to 1.5; evidence is thin and heavily shrunk

stages.name: Quarterback spikes and end-of-half clock management near the goal line
stages.description: A quarterback spike (a throw into the ground to stop the clock) near the end of a half, taken on or inside the opponent's 1-yard line, is a clock-management play and not a pass call chosen against a sneak or run. In play-by-play it is commonly logged as an incomplete pass, and the KXNFL1YDPASS text excludes sacks, scrambles and runs but says nothing about spikes, so whether Kalshi counts one is unstated and is not asserted here. The model therefore carries the spike count separately: the number of end-of-half snaps from the 1, driven by two-minute tempo and timeouts, times the probability the offence spikes. The spike raises the apparent pass rate at the 1 above the coach's pass-call rate and must be separated before fitting coach effects. The play-by-play flag for spikes (a qb_spike field) and its handling are unverified.
stages.distribution: Rare end-of-half Bernoulli per team-game (probability not measured; to recount from play-by-play); strongly concentrated in half-ending drives with timeouts

stages.name: Settlement: official forward pass attempt and positional definition
stages.description: The 1-yard series counts official forward pass attempts recorded in the play-by-play with the line of scrimmage at the snap on or inside the 1; sacks, scrambles and runs do not count, and a pass attempt nullified by penalty counts if officially recorded. The non-QB series needs the passer's position; the sampled text does not define it, so a tight end lining up at quarterback or a backup quarterback listed elsewhere is ambiguous. The probability of Yes is the probability of at least one qualifying event over the game's snaps, with overtime handling unstated. Whether a spike or a fake spike counts as a pass attempt for KXNFL1YDPASS is not stated in the sampled text (u4); the pass_attempt flag semantics (whether sacks are included, how no_play rows are treated) were not verified against the nflverse dictionary (u6).
stages.distribution: Bernoulli outcome; P(Yes) = 1 - P(no qualifying snap) = 1 - exp(-lambda) with lambda overdispersed by coach and by quarterback availability

talent_strength.note: Team strength matters only through how often the offence reaches the 1-yard line; red-zone volume is the proxy.

opponent_matchup.note: Opposing goal-line personnel and stand rate modulate snaps from the 1 and the call; evidence is thin.

role_personnel.note: Goal-line personnel, quarterback mobility and usage shares at the 1 define who gets the ball and whether a sneak replaces a pass.

availability_news.note: Quarterback availability and in-game exit risk drive the emergency non-quarterback pass regime.

coaching_scheme.note: Both events are coach choices; coach and coordinator random effects are the dominant source of variation.

environment.note: Whether wind, cold or precipitation changes goal-line pass calls or trick-play frequency is not measured here and is not assumed negligible; no environment input is staged for these series (u7).

game_context_script.note: Score state and clock shift the call at the 1, fake plays late and quarterback spikes; nfl.script is context (re-based on own-model margins).

pace_volume.note: The number of snaps from the 1 per game is the volume of the 1-yard hazard; field position and red-zone trips supply it.

efficiency_conversion.note: Red-zone conversion decides whether drives stall at the 1 or score before; it matters for snap supply only.

distribution_variance.note: Bernoulli hazard with a heavy-tailed coach distribution; shrinkage must reflect skew.

situational_schedule_motivation.note: Stakes are a plausible but unverified driver, only labelled by seeding stakes; the effect size is unmeasured (u2).

officiating_rules.note: Penalty-nullified attempts count if recorded in the play-by-play per the text; the treatment of spikes is not stated (u4).

settlement_contract.note: Line of scrimmage at the snap, official forward pass attempt and penalty treatment are read from the rules text; non-QB and spike treatment are not defined.

nfl.trick_play_and_goal_line_pass_events.label: Rare play-call events: non-QB pass attempts and pass attempts from the 1-yard line
nfl.trick_play_and_goal_line_pass_events.mechanism: Per-team rates of non-quarterback pass attempts (trick plays, fake punts) and of pass calls on snaps from on or inside the opponent's 1, combined with the expected number of snaps from the 1.
nfl.trick_play_and_goal_line_pass_events.rationale: Both contracts are low-rate Bernoulli events whose base rate differs strongly by coach and personnel (for example a former-quarterback receiver, or a team that favours quarterback sneaks at the 1; both are hypotheses to test, not measured facts); league averages mislead, but team samples are tiny, so heavy shrinkage toward the league rate is essential and stakes may raise trick-play frequency.
nfl.trick_play_and_goal_line_pass_events.measurement: Non-QB pass: count of pass attempts by players whose roster position is not QB per team-game over the last 3 seasons, shrunk to league rate (about 0.15 per game, to recompute) with k=40 team-games, coach random effect; P(any in game) = 1 - exp(-(rate_A + rate_B)). Pass from the 1: expected snaps with yardline_100 <= 1 per team-game (from drives reaching the 1, last 2 seasons, shrink k=30) x team pass share on those snaps (shrink to league about 0.35 with k=25 snaps) counting official forward pass attempts only; sacks, scrambles and runs must be excluded explicitly (whether the nflverse pass_attempt flag already excludes sacks, how no_play rows are treated and how spikes are flagged are UNVERIFIED); P(at least one) by Poisson. As-of kickoff with the active roster.

nfl.end_of_half_goal_line_snap_and_spike.label: End-of-half goal-line snap exposure and quarterback spike probability
nfl.end_of_half_goal_line_snap_and_spike.mechanism: Expected number of snaps on or inside the opponent's 1-yard line in the closing seconds of each half (when a spike can stop the clock) and the probability that such a snap is a quarterback spike rather than a run or pass call.
nfl.end_of_half_goal_line_snap_and_spike.rationale: A spike is a clock-management play, not a pass call chosen against a sneak, and play-by-play commonly logs it as an incomplete pass. If a spike counts for KXNFL1YDPASS it adds attempts that no coach pass-call model explains, and it must be separated from the pass-call rate before fitting coach effects.
nfl.end_of_half_goal_line_snap_and_spike.measurement: From nflverse play-by-play 2015-2025 (the data dictionary lists a qb_spike flag and play_type 'qb_spike'; field semantics to confirm) count, per team-game, snaps with yardline_100 <= 1 and game_seconds_remaining in the half <= 60, and estimate P(spike | such snap) by logistic regression on seconds remaining, timeouts remaining, score differential bucket from the own-model margin distribution (not betting lines), down, and a coach random effect (shrink to league with k=10 snaps). Expected spikes on or inside the 1 per team-game = (expected end-of-half snaps from the 1, from drive success and the drive-reaching-the-1 rate of nfl.redzone and nfl.field_pos) x P(spike). Output separately the expected non-spike pass calls and the spike count so that either reading of the contract can be priced. As-of kickoff.

nfl.qb.reason: A mobile quarterback who sneaks lowers goal-line passes; the starter's availability sets the non-quarterback emergency-pass hazard.

nfl.in_game_exit_risk.reason: Position-agnostic probability of missing more than 25 percent of snaps; it is not quarterback-specific, so the quarterback exit hazard comes from nfl.qb_blowout_pull_hazard and the depth slot model.

nfl.redzone.reason: The 1-yard pass event needs the offence to reach the 1; red-zone trips are the supply side of the hazard.

nfl.field_pos.reason: Short fields from turnovers or returns raise goal-to-go snaps from the 1 without a long drive.

nfl.rz_share.reason: Usage concentration at the goal line separates run-heavy from pass-heavy short-yardage calls.

nfl.formation.reason: Formation charting is the only available evidence for trick-play usage beyond raw counts; limited sample.

nfl.def_personnel.reason: Defensive goal-line packages change the offence's expected value for pass calls at the 1, a second-order matchup effect.

nonlinearities.shape: pass share lowest at exactly the 1-yard line and rising with yards to go out to about the 5-yard line
nonlinearities.why: Snaps from exactly the 1 are dominated by sneaks and short-yardage runs by assumption (to verify), so a team's average goal-to-go pass rate from longer distances overstates its 1-yard pass rate; the response to distance is a steep step near the goal line rather than a linear trend, and the rate must be measured at the 1.

nonlinearities.shape: Bernoulli with a very small per-game probability: P(at least one) = 1 - exp(-lambda), almost linear in lambda for small lambda and saturating for high-volume trick-play teams
nonlinearities.why: With a small per-game rate (the catalog placeholder is about 0.15 per team-game, unverified) the probability of at least one is nearly proportional to the rate, so errors in the coach random effect carry nearly one-for-one into price error, while for a team with several per game it saturates.

nonlinearities.shape: assumed heavy right tail: a minority of coaches and coordinators may account for a large share of trick plays (unverified)
nonlinearities.why: If trick-play usage is concentrated the league mean hides a skewed distribution and the shrinkage prior must be heavy tailed; the degree of concentration has not been measured and is an assumption to test.

catalog_entry.label: NFL league-wide tie and long-field-goal counts
catalog_entry.target: Whether a league-wide count of rare outcomes (tied games in a season or week, made field goals from 60+ yards in a season) reaches a threshold.
catalog_entry.mechanism: Each contract counts a rare event over every game in a window: the number of tied games in the regular season, whether at least one game in a specific week ends tied, and the number of made field goals from 60 or more yards in the regular season. The count is a Poisson-binomial sum of small per-game probabilities over the games remaining in the window (schedule exposure), plus the banked count to date. A tie probability is the lattice mass at zero after regulation times the chance overtime ends level under the current overtime rule; a 60+ make probability is an end-of-half and big-leg attempt hazard times a steeply falling make curve with altitude and kicker-ceiling terms. Rare-event aggregation, rule eras and schedule exposure dominate rather than team production.

Kneel-down, kick-to-tie and go-for-two policy in tied or one-score states late in games changes whether a regulation tie survives into overtime and how often overtime ends level.
Number of games per week, byes and windows define the exposure of a weekly tie contract (Week 2 has a specific game count) and the number of games left in the season count.

Rule and ball regime (K-ball preparation, kickoff regime) shifts the league-wide 60+ attempt and make rates between seasons.

contract.settlement_definition: Three series over the 2026-27 regular season. KXNFLTIES settles Yes if at least 4 games result in a tie across the regular season (floor_strike 4, greater_or_equal); KXNFLWEEKTIE settles Yes if at least one game ends in a tie in Week 2 of the regular season; KXNFL60YARDFGS settles Yes if there are 8+ made field goals from at least 60 yards in the regular season. The sampled rules texts do not state the source of truth, how a postponed or relocated game or a game not completed is treated, or how kick distance is measured; the secondary text of KXNFLTIES says only that it resolves on the total number of tied games. Overtime is implicit in a tie (a regular-season game that ends level after overtime) but not discussed, and playoff games are outside the window by the 'regular season' wording.

rules_evidence.quote: This market resolves based on the total number of games that result in a tie in the 2026-27 Pro Football regular season.

A tie requires a game level after the regular-season overtime period, so the overtime rule and any rule change alter the tie rate; the sampled texts do not mention overtime and the rule in force for 2026-27 was not verified here.

mechanism.summary: All three contracts count a rare event over every game of a window, so the object is a Poisson-binomial sum of small per-game probabilities plus a banked count. The chain starts with schedule exposure (which games remain, how many in the named week), builds a per-game tie probability as the product of the chance of a level score after regulation and the chance overtime ends level under the current rule, models long field goals as an end-of-half and big-leg attempt hazard times a steeply falling make curve with altitude and kicker-ceiling terms, and aggregates with the banked state at the contract strike. The estimate is dominated by rule and ball eras and by a few kickers and venues, not by average team quality, and the uncertainty is the scarcity of events: the league sees only a handful of ties and of 60+ makes per season.

stages.name: Schedule exposure and banked count
stages.description: Each contract sums over the games in its window. For the season count the window is the whole regular season; the games still to play, the banked count to date and the identity of the remaining matchups define the exposure, defined in nfl.league_window_banked_count_and_exposure. For the weekly tie the exposure is only that week's slate, read from the schedule (16 games if no team has a bye that week; Week 2 is not expected to have byes, to confirm from the schedule); the sampled KXNFLWEEKTIE market is already finalized, so the weekly series has no live exposure for that sample. The model needs the as-of time, because a count already at the threshold is settled and a count far below it with few games left is nearly dead. The treatment of postponed or unplayed games is not stated in the sampled text and is carried as a flag.
stages.distribution: Poisson-binomial over remaining games with a banked-count atom; per-game rates are small and not yet sourced (to compute from official results)

stages.name: Per-game tie probability: level after regulation, level after overtime
stages.description: A game is a tie only if the score is level after 60 minutes and the regular-season overtime (a single 10-minute period) also ends level. The first factor is the mass at zero of the margin distribution, highest for close matchups and low-scoring games and corrected for key-number effects; the second depends on the overtime possession rule in force and on coaching decisions late in regulation and in overtime (kneeling, kick-to-tie, going for two). The two factors multiply, so the per-game tie probability is a fraction of a percent, with close games carrying several times the average.
stages.distribution: Per-game tie probability is the product of the regulation-level mass and the overtime-level conditional probability; magnitudes are unsourced placeholders to compute per rule era from official results

stages.name: Long field goals: attempt hazard
stages.description: Made field goals from 60 or more yards need an attempt, and attempts are rare decisions: they occur mostly at the end of halves and games when the offence is outside normal range but time is short, in high-altitude or dome venues, and for kickers with demonstrated range. The attempt hazard per team-game depends on the coach's willingness, kicker ceiling, wind and altitude, the rule and ball regime and the score state (trailing by up to three at the end of a half). League-wide expected attempts are a sum over team-games of this hazard. The attempt hazard is split into 60-64, 65-69 and 70+ bands so that it matches the 60-yard contract threshold; the 65+ detail input covers the tail only.
stages.distribution: Attempts per team-game are very small and clustered at end-of-half situations; the league total over the season is a count whose size is not sourced here (to count from play-by-play); the earlier per-team-game range and season range quoted were inconsistent and are withdrawn

stages.name: Long field goals: make probability beyond 60 yards
stages.description: Given an attempt, the make probability falls steeply with distance past about 55 yards, rises with altitude and a tailwind, is truncated by the kicker's physical ceiling, and shifts by season with the kicking-ball and rule regime. The expected count of makes is attempts times this curve summed over kickers and venues; because few kickers can make 60+, a handful of leg-strong kickers contribute most of the expected count. Preseason and warm-up evidence gives weak signal on who has the leg.
stages.distribution: Per-attempt make probability falls steeply with distance beyond 55 yards (levels by band are unsourced placeholders to refit by era); the season count is a thin right-skewed count

stages.name: Aggregation, banked state and settlement
stages.description: The final probability is the tail mass of the banked count plus the Poisson-binomial draw from remaining games, evaluated at each strike. The live series are N+ thresholds (sampled strikes 4+ ties and 8+ long makes), so the output must be a monotone nested distribution across strikes, not one strike in isolation. Dependence between games is weak but present through shared rule regime and weather; the rule era and the data source must be fixed. Whether an unplayed or abandoned game counts is not stated for these series; postponed games are carried with a flag, not assumed. Whether a made fair-catch free-kick field goal of 60+ yards counts for KXNFL60YARDFGS is not stated (u4).
stages.distribution: Season tie count and 60+ make count are approximately Poisson-binomial with unsourced means (to compute from official results by era) and a heavy right tail for makes from a few kickers and venues

nfl.league_window_banked_count_and_expos.label: League-window banked count and remaining-game exposure (ties and 60+ yard makes)
nfl.league_window_banked_count_and_expos.mechanism: For a league-wide count over a window, the number of qualifying events already banked at an as-of time and the list of games still to be played in the window with the features that set each game's event probability.
nfl.league_window_banked_count_and_expos.rationale: The league tie and long-kick contracts are banked-plus-remaining sums. The player-season accrual inputs of the season-stat blueprint describe individual players, not league-wide events, so the banked count, games remaining, the as-of rule and the treatment of unplayed games need their own definition.
nfl.league_window_banked_count_and_expos.measurement: At as-of time T: banked_ties = number of regular-season games with final status completed before T whose official final score is level; banked_60 = number of made field goals with official kick length >= 60 yards in regular-season games before T (flag free-kick field goals separately because their treatment by the contract is unstated). Remaining exposure = list of regular-season games in the window not yet completed at T (week, teams, roof, altitude, kickoff, expected margin from nfl.own_team_rating_market_free, kicker identities), with a flag for postponed, relocated or suspended games and the week they move to. For a weekly contract the window is that week's games only. Unplayed or cancelled games are flagged STATUS_UNSTATED and the output carries the count with and without them. Output (banked, N_remaining, per-game feature rows) as of T; recompute after every completed game.

nfl.fg_attempt_hazard_by_distance_band_6.label: Field-goal attempt hazard by distance band at 60+ yards (60-64, 65-69, 70+)
nfl.fg_attempt_hazard_by_distance_band_6.mechanism: Per team-game hazard of a field-goal attempt of at least 60 yards, split into 60-64, 65-69 and 70+ bands by the situations in which such attempts are chosen (end of half, trailing by up to three, short clock, venue and wind), the head coach and the kicker's demonstrated range.
nfl.fg_attempt_hazard_by_distance_band_6.rationale: The contract counts made kicks of 60 yards or more and most expected makes are likely at the short end of the range, so an attempt hazard defined only for 65+ yards misses the main contributors; a band-specific hazard is the attempt side of attempts times make probability for the contract threshold.
nfl.fg_attempt_hazard_by_distance_band_6.measurement: From play-by-play over the last 4 seasons count attempts with official kick length in each band per team-game and qualifying situations (game_seconds_remaining in half <= 20, offence with yardline_100 between 43 and 62 so that the kick length, about yardline_100 + 17 yards, is 60 to 79 yards (a 60-yard kick is snapped from about the opponent 43), score differential in {-3..0} at half end, plus venue altitude and roof); estimate P(attempt in band | situation) by a hierarchical logit with head coach and kicker random effects (kicker max made kick, 60+ history, wind, rule era including the K-ball regime of nfl.kicking_ball_and_fg_rule_era), shrinking coach rates to the league with 15 qualifying situations of prior weight. Output expected attempts per band for each remaining team-game and the league total for the remaining schedule; make probability by band comes from nfl.long_fg_attempt_and_make_model and nfl.kicker_ceiling_range_tail. As-of kickoff with the active kicker.

nonlinearities.why: Beyond a kicker's ceiling the make probability does not fall smoothly to zero but collapses, so a handful of strong-legged kickers account for almost all expected 60+ makes and the league-wide count behaves like a sum over a few contributors.

catalog_entry.label: NFL team event hazards over a multi-week schedule window
catalog_entry.target: Whether a named team records at least one occurrence of a defensive event (an interception) in any regular-season game inside a stated window of weeks after issuance.
catalog_entry.mechanism: The outcome is an at-least-once event over a list of future games, so its probability is one minus the expected product of per-game zero-event probabilities. The chain is: define the games in the window (after issuance, before the stated week, byes, a game possibly in progress at issuance), draw each opponent's starting quarterback, compute each game's event hazard from opposing dropbacks, the team's defensive rate and the opposing quarterback's rate, and aggregate across games with a shared defensive-quality factor that makes games dependent. The result is dominated by the number of games and the thin no-event tail, not by one game's strength.

contract.settlement_definition: One series sampled, KXNFLNEXTINT (status finalized, strike_type structured). The primary text settles Yes if the named team (the New York J team in the sample) records an interception in a regular season game after issuance and before Week 8 of the 2026-27 season; the secondary text says that if the team does not record an interception in that window the market resolves to No. The sampled text does not say how a game in progress at issuance is handled, whether Week 8 itself is excluded beyond 'before Week 8', how overtime, postponement or a postponed game outside the window are handled, or, in the sampled rules text, the source of truth (series metadata reportedly names one, see settlement_data_source).

rules_evidence.quote: records an interception in a regular season game after issuance and before Week 8
rules_evidence.establishes: The event is at least one interception by the named team in a regular season game inside the window; playoff games are outside by the 'regular season' wording and the window ends before Week 8.

rules_evidence.quote: does not record an interception after issuance and before Week 8 of the 2026-27 season, then the market resolves to No
rules_evidence.establishes: The complementary outcome in the secondary text: no interception inside the window resolves No.

variants_and_edge_cases: The sampled series is one rung of a nested ladder: a reviewer reports from Kalshi API metadata (not in the sampled rules text, unverified) rungs before Week 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 14, 16 and 'anytime' for one team, windows of about 1 to 17 games, all opened before Week 1 and now finalized; the model must output a monotone nested distribution across rungs.
'After issuance' is not defined for a game in progress at issuance; if listings were opened before Week 1 the case does not arise for them, but the model carries both readings for in-season listings.
The window ends 'before Week 8': games in weeks 1 to 7 qualify on the plain reading; a bye removes a game, and a postponed game moved past the window would drop out; neither is stated in the sample.

The sampled text restricts the event to a regular season game and does not mention overtime, an interception on a two-point try, a penalty-nullified interception (nflverse has a play_deleted flag, not checked), or later statistical corrections.

mechanism.summary: The outcome is an at-least-once event over a list of future games, so its probability is one minus the expected product of per-game zero-event probabilities. The chain is: define the games in the window (after issuance, before the stated week, byes, a game possibly in progress at issuance), draw each opponent's starting quarterback, compute each game's event hazard from opposing dropbacks, the team's defensive rate and the opposing quarterback's rate, and aggregate across games with a shared defensive-quality factor that makes games dependent. The result is dominated by the number of games and the thin no-event tail, not by one game's strength. The series is the only one in its family sampled, so the chain is derived from the contract wording and first principles and the cross-game dependence is a modelling assumption to be tested, not an observed fact.

stages.name: Window definition: games after issuance and before the stated week
stages.description: The contract is settled by the games the named team plays after the market's issuance and before the end of a stated week. The sampled market ends before Week 8, and the reviewer reports a ladder of rungs for one team (before Week 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 14, 16 and 'anytime'), all opened before Week 1 and now finalized (reported, not in the sampled text, unverified). The windows are therefore nested and range from one game to a whole season of about seventeen games, so the number of games per rung, byes, flex or postponement and, for any in-season listing, a game in progress at issuance decide the exposure. The number of games in the window is the largest driver of the probability, since each extra game multiplies the no-event probability by a further factor below one.
stages.distribution: Number of window games per rung is a small to moderate integer (about 1 to 17 across rungs); rungs are nested events so the probability is non-decreasing in the rung and rises steeply with the number of games

stages.name: Opposing starting quarterbacks across the window
stages.description: Each game has an opposing quarterback who may not be the current starter by the time the game is played: injuries, benching and promotion change the starter and a backup may throw interceptions at a different rate (unverified). The model needs the as-of probability distribution over each opponent's starter per game, widening with the weeks ahead, rather than the current depth chart. Opponent quarterbacks are the main game-to-game source of variation in the hazard. Over the longest rungs the opposing starter is uncertain for many weeks, so the starter distribution is a mixture that widens with weeks ahead.
stages.distribution: Per game the starter is a discrete mixture (starter, backup, change) with a small backup probability that grows with weeks ahead

stages.name: Per-game interception hazard
stages.description: For one game the expected interception count is the opposing dropbacks (opposing plays from the pace and total-plays models times the opposing dropback rate from PROE) times the league interception rate per dropback times two ratio multipliers: the named team's defensive multiplier (quarterback-adjusted base from nfl.opp_def_int_propensity, adjusted for defensive-back availability and coverage-scheme changes through nfl.def_personnel and nfl.coverage_scheme, which measure availability and scheme and not ball skills) and the opposing quarterback's multiplier (net of defences faced). Pressure and trailing script for the opponent raise it and wind lowers it. Per-attempt rates regress strongly to the mean, so the hazard varies in a narrow band. The per-game probability of at least one is one minus the exponential of minus the expected count under a Poisson reading; overdispersion is handled in stage s4.
stages.distribution: Per-game count approximately Poisson with a small mean; the per-game probability of at least one is an unsourced placeholder to be computed from play-by-play

stages.name: Survival product with a shared defensive factor
stages.description: S(W), the probability of no event through rung W, is the expected product across the games of that rung of the per-game zero-event probabilities, taken over a shared latent defensive-quality factor and over the starter scenarios. All rungs are computed from the same draws, so S(W) is non-increasing in W and the ladder of Yes probabilities is monotone: before Week 4 cannot be below before Week 2. Independent games understate the chance of a long drought because a team with a truly low takeaway rate has a low rate in every game; the shared factor fattens that tail. The output is P(at least one) for every rung, with and without the shared factor, recomputed after every game.
stages.distribution: P(No) = E over shared factor and starter scenarios of a product of exponentials; heavier no-event tail than an independent product

stages.name: Settlement: interception statistic, regular season, No on none
stages.description: The sampled text counts an interception recorded by the named team in a regular season game inside the window and resolves No if there is none. It does not say how a game in progress at issuance, an overtime interception, an interception on a two-point try, a postponed game, or a data source is treated; the model carries those as readings and reports the spread. The sample status is finalized with no postponement sentence, so nothing is asserted about a fair-price rule for this series.
stages.distribution: Binary outcome with Yes mass almost 1 for long windows; the settlement readings change the probability only when N_g is small

nfl.team_window_game_exposure.label: Team game list and issuance state inside a multi-week event window
nfl.team_window_game_exposure.mechanism: The list of regular-season games a named team still plays between a market's issuance and the end of its stated window, with byes, kickoff times, the state of any game in progress at issuance and the probability distribution over each opponent's starting quarterback.
nfl.team_window_game_exposure.rationale: An at-least-once event over a window is a product over the games in it, so the number of games, which of them are home or road, which opponents they are and whether a game is already under way at issuance are first-order inputs. None of the player-level inputs defines the window; the contract text says only 'after issuance and before Week 8'.
nfl.team_window_game_exposure.measurement: From the official schedule as of the market's issuance timestamp T, for team t build the rung ladder of windows: for each end week W in {2,4,6,8,12,14,16} and 'anytime' (the whole regular season) the window of rung W is the set of regular-season games with week < W (these rungs were reported by a reviewer from Kalshi API metadata, not by the sampled rules text, and are unverified); compute N_g(W) for every rung (from 1 to about 17 games) so nested windows share the same game list. For each game record week, kickoff time, opponent, home or road, roof and bye weeks (a bye contributes no game). Game g is inside a window if kickoff_g > T; a game in progress at T is flagged IN_PROGRESS and carried with both readings (counted with remaining plays only versus excluded) because the sampled text does not say; the reviewer reports the nine sampled markets were all opened before Week 1 (unverified), in which case no game is in progress at issuance. Attach to each game the as-of distribution over the opponent's starting quarterback from nfl.qb and nfl.weekly_qb_depth_slot_model (widening with weeks ahead, up to 17 weeks for the longest rung). Recompute whenever the schedule changes (flex, postponement, relocation) and flag postponed games and their new week. Output the game table with features and the N_g(W) ladder.

nfl.window_hazard_survival_with_game_cor.label: Window survival product with cross-game dependence
nfl.window_hazard_survival_with_game_cor.mechanism: Turns per-game event hazards into the probability of at least one event over each nested window of a rung ladder as one minus the expected product of per-game zero-event probabilities, averaging over shared uncertainty (the team's defensive quality, scheme changes, quarterback injuries) that links the games.
nfl.window_hazard_survival_with_game_cor.rationale: Multiplying independent per-game probabilities overstates how fast the probability of at least one event approaches one when the games share a common unknown such as the defence's true rate; the shared factor fattens the no-event tail, which is exactly the part of the distribution that prices a Yes contract near the top.
nfl.window_hazard_survival_with_game_cor.measurement: Per game g for team t: expected event count lambda_g = D_g x p0 x m_def(t) x m_qb(q_g), where D_g = expected opposing dropbacks (opposing plays from nfl.pace and nfl.total_plays_state_model times the opposing dropback rate; nfl.proe is a pass-rate-over-expected input whose pass-attempt versus dropback definition is not verified, so the dropback rate must be re-measured as qb_dropback per play, sacks and scrambles included, and p0 is defined per qb_dropback to match), p0 = league interceptions per dropback, m_def(t) = the named team's defensive interception multiplier relative to the league (a ratio, not a rate): a base multiplier from nfl.opp_def_int_propensity (already adjusted for the quality of quarterbacks faced) times an availability-and-scheme adjustment A(t) as of T, where A(t) is estimated by regressing past team interception multipliers on the snap-weighted availability of cornerbacks and safeties from nfl.def_personnel (injury and absence vintages) and on the change in man/zone and single-high/two-high shell rates from nfl.coverage_scheme versus the base period (these inputs measure availability and scheme, not ball skills, so ball-skill differences enter only through the team's own past takeaways), and m_qb(q_g) = the opposing quarterback's multiplier relative to the league (a ratio) from nfl.int_rate, estimated net of the defences he has faced; the two multipliers are ratios so that no per-attempt rate is multiplied by another and the quarterback is not counted twice (if m_def were not quarterback-adjusted it must not be combined with m_qb). The team's takeaway rate uses the interception flag only (fumble recoveries excluded); nfl.turnovers is a regression benchmark, not the rate. Draw a shared log-multiplier u_t ~ Normal(0, tau^2) for the defence (tau to be fitted from between-season variation of team interception rates after shrinkage) and draw each game's opposing starter from its as-of distribution. Survival to the end of rung W: S(W) = E[ product over games with week < W of exp(-lambda_g exp(u_t)) ]; compute every rung from the same draws so S(W) is non-increasing in W and P(at least one by W) = 1 - S(W) is monotone across the nested rungs. Report with and without the shared factor. As-of issuance timestamp and recomputed after each game.

nonlinearities.shape: saturating in the number of games: P(at least one) approaches 1 geometrically with window length, slower under the shared factor
nonlinearities.why: With six or seven window games the independent product leaves almost no No mass, so the contract price is decided by the small tail where the shared defensive factor and quarterback scenarios matter; small errors in the tail are a large relative error in the No price.

nonlinearities.shape: regression toward the mean: recent interception rates are shrunk strongly, so the response to the observed rate is concave
nonlinearities.why: Quarterback interception rates carry little persistent signal over short samples, so the model must shrink and the implied per-game hazard varies only in a narrow band across quarterbacks.

nonlinearities.shape: possible mixture of a starter-hazard component and a backup-hazard component (shape unverified)
nonlinearities.why: If backups differ from starters in interception rate (not verified here) the hazard across games is a mixture with a small second component; the size and sign of the difference are an empirical question and should not be assumed.
